# **Computational Modeling of Occupancy and Energy Dynamics in Vertically Stacked Supertall Buildings: Paradigms, Services, and Simulation Failure Modes**

The rapid hybridization of programming within high-density urban centers has established the vertically mixed-use high-rise (MUHR) as a dominant architectural typology under compact city theory.1 These structures typically concentrate retail podiums at their base, stack multi-tenant commercial offices in the middle, and place luxury hospitality, serviced apartments, or residential units at the upper elevations, culminating in public observation decks or mechanical crowns.1 According to the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH), a tall building is classified as mixed-use if it contains two or more major functions, where each function occupies at least 15% of the total floor area.1 Historical trends demonstrate an accelerating adoption of this typology: between 1924 and 2000, only 96 mixed-use towers above 150 meters were constructed globally, whereas the period from 2000 to 2016 saw the completion of 499 such structures.1 Within this category, residential and serviced apartments represent the prevailing dominant function in 50% of buildings, followed by hospitality (34%) and commercial offices (17%).1 While dual-function towers represent approximately 85% of this stock, only about 60 structures globally combine three or more distinct programs, placing them at the peak of structural, thermodynamic, and operational complexity.1  
This structural and programmatic density presents significant challenges for conventional Urban Building Energy Modeling (UBEM) and Building Performance Simulation (BPS) frameworks.4 Modeling a single building as an isolated, uniform entity fails to capture the complex thermal, mechanical, and human behavioral interactions characteristic of stacked, multi-tenant supertall structures.6 High-fidelity building energy models must navigate vertically shifting microclimatic boundary conditions 7, spatiotemporal cross-use occupancy correlations 4, complex vertical circulation systems 10, and the physical realities of the vertical stack effect.12

## **Vertical Microclimatic Boundary Conditions and Envelope Dynamics**

A critical limitation of conventional building energy simulation is the reliance on ground-level meteorological data.7 In supertall buildings, climatic variables such as dry-bulb temperature, wind velocity, and atmospheric pressure change significantly along the vertical axis.7 The standard atmospheric temperature lapse rate of approximately ![][image1] suggests that a 500-meter tower will experience a temperature differential of over ![][image2] between its base and crown.7 This variation is highly season- and climate-specific, often characterized by complex local phenomena such as vertical temperature inversions that linear lapse rates cannot convey.7 Wind velocity also increases non-linearly with altitude due to planetary boundary layer shear, compounding convective heat loss at higher levels while increasing wind pressure on the facade.7  
Standard simulations that neglect these altitude-dependent variations introduce substantial errors.14 Comparative studies of the 541-meter One World Trade Center revealed that incorporating altitude-specific temperature, wind, and air density profiles results in up to a 13% reduction in simulated heating and cooling loads, with localized cooling energy reductions reaching up to 26% on upper floors.7 To capture these boundaries, researchers utilize weather files derived from recorded upper-air atmospheric parameters (e.g., radiosonde data) coupled with complex mesoscale climate models.7

| Parameter | Ground-Level / Base Zone | Upper Supertall Zone (\>300m) | Primary Impact on Simulation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Ambient Temperature** | Higher (affected by urban heat island and ground reflection) 7 | Lower (subject to atmospheric lapse rates and temperature inversions) 7 | Reductions in cooling demands of 6% to 26%; elevation of local heating loads in winter.7 |
| **Wind Speed** | Lower (buffered by surrounding urban canopy and roughness) 7 | High (unobstructed boundary layer wind velocity) 7 | Escalated convective heat transfer coefficients across the envelope; complex pressure-driven infiltration.14 |
| **Barometric Pressure** | Standard Atmospheric (![][image3]) | Reduced (progressively lower air density) 14 | Altered HVAC fan efficiencies, reduced volumetric air-mass flow rates, and shifts in moisture capacity.7 |
| **Microclimatic Shading** | High (subject to complex shadows from adjacent urban structures) 14 | Negligible (protrudes above the urban canopy layer) 14 | Elevated direct solar radiation, driving high solar heat gains requiring optimized glazing SHGC.14 |

These microclimatic forces interact directly with structural massing and envelope geometries.3 Programmatic transitions from deep-floor-plate offices to shallow-floor-plate residential zones are typically navigated via physical step-backs and setbacks.3 This vertical variation in floor-plate depth changes the local surface-area-to-volume ratio (![][image4]) and window-to-wall ratios (WWR) along the tower height.16  
Energy models must navigate strict energy conservation codes alongside design objectives.18 For example, California's Title 24 code limits standard commercial WWR to 40%.18 During the design of the Wilshire Grand in Los Angeles, eQUEST simulations demonstrated that expanding the WWR to 60% would increase overall energy usage by 5.1% and result in $188,737 in annual energy cost penalties, leading the team to select a balanced 50% WWR.18 In contrast, hot-arid climates require distinct parameter optimizations.17 Parametric Rhino/Grasshopper workflows coupled with EnergyPlus for residential designs in New Cairo, Egypt, showed that cooling setpoints and building geometry are the dominant drivers of annual energy variance, whereas standard envelope insulation parameters exhibit minimal influence within code-compliant ranges.17  
The introduction of external facade features, such as balconies, further complicates thermal performance.15 Generative design algorithms focusing on thermal comfort and daylighting reveal that while modest balcony extensions can reduce cooling loads, a 100% vertical distribution of separate balconies creates extensive envelope thermal bridges and disrupts airflow boundaries, increasing the overall heating and cooling demands.15

## **Spatiotemporal Cross-Use Occupancy Dynamics and Sensor Fusion**

The primary source of uncertainty in urban-scale and high-rise energy simulations is the stochastic nature of occupant behavior.19 Standard engineering models typically rely on static, deterministic schedules (e.g., ASHRAE, regional calculation standards, or the UK National Calculation Methodology) that assume uniform, non-interactive occupancy profiles.9

### **The Fallacy of Decoupled Schedules**

Static occupant schedules assume that all zones of a given use type operate in physical isolation, ignoring the dynamic movement of individuals within a mixed-use ecosystem.4 In a vertically stacked tower, the same physical occupant represents a continuous load profile that transitions between different spatial programs throughout the day.4 For instance, an occupant absent from their commercial office workstation during lunch hours is highly likely to be present in the retail podium's food court or restaurant zones.4  
Applying isolated, standard schedules to both the office and retail zones simultaneously results in "occupant duplication" or artificial load isolation.4 This decoupled approach fails to capture the correlated peaks and off-peaks of internal heat gains, leading to unrealistic coincidental peak loads.20 When these uncoordinated peaks are aggregated, building energy models overpredict peak demand, which can lead to oversized HVAC systems, excessive capital costs, and reduced part-load operational efficiency.4

### **Capturing Spatiotemporal Vibrancy via Mobile Positioning Data**

To capture realistic occupant trajectories, contemporary researchers leverage high-resolution empirical data, such as cellular tower signaling, global positioning system (GPS) logs, and Point of Interest (POI) databases.9 These data sources act as proxies for local vibrancy and pedestrian flows.23  
By analyzing mobile positioning data collected within mixed-use districts, modelers can track the transition probabilities of occupants moving between different building functions.9 The raw device counts extracted from specific spatial coordinate zones are scaled up to match actual population metrics using dissemination area statistics 9:  
![][image5]  
These scaled profiles are subsequently clustered based on floor areas, generating representative stochastic schedules that capture real-world operational diversity and spatial interaction.9

### **Multi-Sensor Fusion and Real-Time Calibration**

To validate and calibrate these stochastic schedules in real-time, high-fidelity models integrate multi-sensor fusion systems.24 These frameworks combine WiFi connections, CO2 environmental sensors, smart meters, and unobtrusive radio-frequency (RF) trackers.20 For example, 24-GHz Continuous Wave (CW) radar networks integrated with Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) and power spectrum analysis can count sedentary and mobile occupants with up to 92.7% accuracy.25 Knowing the precise, real-time number of occupants allows building automation systems to implement demand-controlled ventilation (DCV) in highly transient zones like lobbies, open offices, and retail outlets, maximizing HVAC efficiency while maintaining indoor air quality.25  
Integrating WiFi-derived occupancy and plug-load profiles into energy models has been shown to reduce the model's Coefficient of Variation of the Root Mean Square Error (CV(RMSE)) from 37% to 24%, bridging the gap between estimated and actual consumption.26 In a higher-education office building within London's Bloomsbury district, an energy-data-driven occupancy model reduced annual heating demand estimation errors to ![][image6], compared to ![][image7] and ![][image8] errors for standard-based and stochastic models, respectively.21

### **Human Behavioral Discrepancies Across Mixed Uses**

A critical hurdle in modeling stacked towers is that the same human occupant displays divergent behavioral patterns, expectations, and control interactions depending on whether they are in a residential, hotel, or commercial office zone.28 In residential apartments, actions such as window blind operation, lighting adjustments, and window opening are highly subjective and driven by personal comfort perceptions, cultural expectations, and direct responsibility for utility bills.28 Occupants in these zones frequently deploy personal heating or cooling devices, which can dramatically alter localized thermal demands.28  
Conversely, in commercial office environments, comfort expectations are narrower, and occupants operate under institutional constraints, such as corporate dress codes.30 Furthermore, office workers are often physically detached from system controls (e.g., thermostat setpoints or window operations), leading to miscommunication with building managers and reliance on centralized HVAC automation.30 In university or highly diverse public settings, cultural variations in indoor comfort expectations introduce another layer of behavioral stochasticity.28  
These behavioral discrepancies create operational frictions at physical and mechanical interfaces.6 In a mixed-use tower, commercial offices require quiet operations during daytime business hours, while residential units require strict quiet hours during nights and weekends.6 Scheduling major mechanical plant maintenance, cooling tower water treatments, or loading dock deliveries requires strict spatiotemporal coordination to prevent noise and vibration propagation across residential floor plates.6  
Furthermore, distinct ventilation paths must be maintained; for instance, restaurant exhaust from retail podiums must be hydraulically isolated and treated to prevent cooking odors from infiltrating residential units above.6 Modelers must account for these boundaries by segmenting common area maintenance (CAM) zones and tagging every mechanical asset with its corresponding use-type operational schedule.6

| Use-Type Program | Primary Occupancy Window | HVAC Control Strategy | Typical Internal Heat Gain | Primary Mechanical Friction Point |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Retail Podium** | 10:00 AM – 10:00 PM 6 | Central VAV with Demand-Controlled Ventilation (DCV) 13 | High (dense occupancy, intense display lighting) 31 | Kitchen exhaust odor and grease migration to residential zones.6 |
| **Commercial Office** | 08:00 AM – 06:00 PM 6 | Central VAV with night setbacks and static setpoints 13 | Moderate (computers, lighting, paper systems) 31 | Elevator peak traffic overlap with residential morning departures.6 |
| **Hotel / Residential** | 24 Hours (Peak: 6:00 PM – 8:00 AM) 6 | Local Fan Coil Units (FCU) or VRF with local thermostats 13 | Low to Moderate (cooking, local appliances, laundry) 17 | Noise and vibration propagation from central plant operations during quiet hours.6 |

## **Modeling Architectures: Shared-Backbone Multi-Task Paradigms vs. Decoupled Sub-Models**

When simulating vertically stacked structures, researchers must choose between two primary modeling paradigms: maintaining isolated, decoupled sub-models for each use type, or deploying an integrated, shared-backbone multi-task architecture.32

### **Decoupled Sub-Models and Geometric Simplification**

The traditional approach to mixed-use high-rise simulation relies on bottom-up physics-based UBEM workflows, utilizing engines such as CityEnergyAnalyst, DistrictGenerator, or SimStadt.5 In this paradigm, buildings are represented using standardized "archetypes" containing fixed thermodynamic envelopes and decoupled schedule templates assigned to each distinct use block.5 To reduce computational complexity and simulation time, modelers implement geometric simplification strategies.36  
A common method is the grouping of thermal zones, where multiple rooms or entire floors with similar thermal properties and orientation are merged into a single zone.36 For instance, a tower can be simplified into one perimeter and one core zone per floor, or grouped into up to three vertical zones representing the ground, middle, and upper blocks.36 While grouping identical apartments or office suites can reduce simulation runtimes by up to 30%, oversimplification introduces substantial errors, underestimating annual heating and cooling demands by 14% to 26% due to the dampening of localized thermal dynamics and orientation-specific solar gains.37

### **The Shared-Backbone Multi-Task Framework**

To balance computational efficiency with the accuracy of coupled interactions, advanced models utilize Multi-Task Learning (MTL).33 Under this framework, a single, high-dimensional model shares its underlying parameter space—the "shared backbone"—across multiple target prediction tasks (e.g., forecasting heating, cooling, and electrical demand across multiple stacked program zones simultaneously).33 A shared selective state-space model (such as the Mamba architecture) or a Transformer-based encoder is deployed to capture the joint temporal dynamics of the building.33

### **Multi-Objective Generative Optimization and Control**

To determine optimal physical configurations and control strategies across these complex state spaces, researchers couple MTL frameworks with multi-objective optimization algorithms, such as NSGA-III or Kriging surrogate models.38 These tools identify Pareto-optimal solutions that balance capital costs, operational energy consumption, and indoor comfort while maintaining code compliance.38 For instance, integrating Kriging surrogates in residential retrofits has demonstrated cost-effective EUI reductions of up to 20%.41  
At the operational scale, Multi-Task Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) frameworks, such as the RECA system, are deployed.42 This framework utilizes a Q-network with a shared embedding layer that learns occupant locations and tracks resource-space relationships using a tripartite graph of energy systems, spaces, and occupants.42 RECA simultaneously optimizes energy, thermal comfort, and indoor air quality by issuing coordinated real-time recommendations.42 Rather than relying solely on automated temperature setpoint adjustments, the system engages occupants directly, recommending temporary movements to underutilized shared spaces or neighboring thermal zones to reduce HVAC loads.42

### **Deep Generative Approaches for Stochastic Profiles**

To synthesize realistic, non-homogenous occupancy profiles for the individual task heads, deep generative architectures have replaced static schedules.43 Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and Flow-Matching/Diffusion models are the primary techniques evaluated in this domain.43

| Generative Architecture | Operational Mechanism | Key Strengths | Documented Limitations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)** | Learns a continuous latent space of occupancy distributions via an encoder-decoder network.43 | Highly stable training trajectory; generates smooth, physically plausible baseline profiles.43 | Tends to underfit high-frequency load variations; generates blurred peak transitions.43 |
| **Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)** | Adopts a zero-sum game between a generator and a discriminative network to synthesize profiles.43 | Captures sharp temporal peaks and realistic extreme-use scenarios.43 | Highly sensitive to hyperparameter tuning; prone to mode collapse and training instability.43 |
| **Regularized Adversarial Fine-Tuning (RAFT-VAE-GAN)** | Combines the structural stability of VAEs with the realistic sample generation of GANs.43 | Overcomes mode collapse and underfitting; generates highly accurate multivariate operational profiles.43 | High computational complexity; requires robust training datasets.43 |
| **Intention-Conditioned Flow Matching (InFOM)** | Progressively refines noise distributions into structured trajectories conditioned on latent user intentions (![][image29]).45 | Captures long-term temporal dependencies; handles highly heterogeneous datasets.45 | High computational overhead during the reverse sampling process.49 |

## **Vertical Circulation and Core Thermodynamic Space Modeling**

The core of a supertall mixed-use tower is a highly complex service column housing vertical transport systems, plumbing, electrical high-voltage risers, and primary mechanical ductwork.10 High-fidelity energy models must treat these service spaces as active thermodynamic zones.13

### **Core Geometry and Elevators as Thermal and Electrical Loads**

In supertall buildings, the core occupies a substantial percentage of the floor plate, often presenting a structural trade-off between maximizing leasable area and ensuring lateral stiffness via outrigger systems.10 Elevators are among the most area-consuming and energy-intensive elements in these cores, accounting for 5% to 15% of a tower's total electrical consumption.10 Modern high-speed traction elevators utilize solid-state variable-voltage, variable-frequency (VVVF) drives with permanent magnet motors and energy recovery modules.11 Regenerative drives capture the potential energy released during braking cycles (e.g., when a heavily loaded cab descends or an empty cab ascends) and return it to the building's internal electrical grid.11  
Beyond direct electrical consumption, elevators act as localized thermal loads.50 The heat rejected from hoistway motors, mechanical braking friction, and guide-rail resistance is dissipated directly into the core zones.50 Standard energy models that omit this heat dissipation underestimate core zone temperatures.50 Modeling the integration of energy-efficient gearless traction elevators can show an overall EUI reduction of up to 20%, driven not only by reduced direct motor consumption but also by lower mechanical room heat loads, which reduces the local cooling demands on HVAC systems.50

### **Airflow Dynamics and CONTAM Co-Simulation**

Supertall structures act as giant thermal chimneys due to the vertical stack effect.12 During winter, cold, dense outdoor air enters the lower levels through entrance doors and envelope infiltration, warms up, and rises rapidly through vertical shafts (elevator hoistways, stairwells, and mechanical utility shafts), escaping through the upper levels.13 In summer, this process is reversed, though typically less intense.52 This movement creates substantial pressure differentials across elevator doors, causing doors to bind in their tracks and fail to close, while generating severe drafts and heating difficulties on lower floors.52  
Standard multi-zone energy modeling engines, such as EnergyPlus, utilize the Airflow Network (AFN) model to calculate inter-zone air mass flows.12 However, validation studies reveal that the AFN model often fails to realistically represent unstable vertical airflow patterns and high-velocity drafts in the presence of continuous vertical shafts.12 To resolve this limitation, modelers employ co-simulation between EnergyPlus and CONTAM—a specialized multizone airflow and contaminant transport analysis program.12 CONTAM calculates detailed mass flow rates and pressure differentials at each timestep 12:  
![][image30]  
These mass flows are dynamically exchanged with the EnergyPlus thermal zones via coupling modules (such as Type 97 in TRNSYS or runtime API bindings in EnergyPlus), ensuring that the thermal energy balance equations are solved using realistic, pressure-driven inter-zone air exchange rates.12

### **Mechanical Zoning and Riser Configurations**

To manage these vertical pressure differentials and limit duct and pipe sizes, mechanical engineers divide supertall buildings into separate vertical HVAC zones, typically spanning 10 to 15 stories each.13 Central chilled water plants distribute conditioned water through massive vertical risers to local mechanical floors situated at strategic intervals.13 These mechanical floors house local air handling units (AHUs), pumping stations, and heat exchangers.13  
A critical mechanical design decision is whether to supply conditioned air from these centralized mechanical rooms serving multiple floors or to deploy local floor-by-floor fan rooms.52 While centralized systems offer economies of scale and simplified maintenance, they occupy valuable shaft area and present challenges in maintaining static pressure control over long vertical distances.13 Conversely, floor-by-floor fan rooms enhance tenant-level zoning and simplify pressure control but demand higher spatial footprint allocation within the leasable area on each individual floor plate.13

## **Systemic Simulation Failure Modes and Calibration Pitfalls**

The extreme complexity of supertall mixed-use buildings increases the risk of simulation failure modes, which can lead to a significant energy performance gap (EPG) between designed and operational consumption.4

### **Systematic Double-Counting of Energy Conservation Measures**

A frequent error in conceptual and deep retrofit modeling is the double-counting of projected energy savings when assessing Energy Conservation Measures (ECMs) sequentially.27 If an analyst evaluates envelope insulation upgrades, variable frequency drive supply fans, and demand-controlled ventilation (DCV) as isolated measures, the cumulative savings will often exceed the physical limits of the building.27 To prevent this, advanced modeling protocols, such as those used in the DOE Building Energy Asset Score, require that subsequent ECM evaluations be simulated on a progressively modified baseline.27 The savings of a secondary upgrade must be calculated *assuming all prior upgrades have already been implemented*.27  
Double-counting also occurs during energy feedstock boundary definitions.58 In integrated co-generation systems or waste-heat recovery loops within a supertall core, energy must be counted on its *first use*.58 For example, natural gas consumed in a combined heat and power (CHP) plant to generate electricity is counted as first-use energy.58 The secondary capture of generator exhaust gas to provide domestic hot water must not be counted as a new energy source, as this duplicates the primary input and artificially inflates the building's thermal efficiency.58

### **Overfitting and Diversity Decay in Stochastic Models**

When training stochastic multi-head neural networks to predict occupancy and load trajectories, modelers frequently rely on the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function.59 However, optimizing solely for MSE forces the network's multiple heads to converge toward a single, smoothed average trajectory.59 This mathematical convergence causes a failure mode known as *diversity decay*.59  
While the smoothed average profile may show low error metrics over a multi-month period, it systematically dampens the high-frequency peaks and valleys characteristic of actual occupant behavior.20 Consequently, the simulation fails to predict realistic peak electrical and cooling demands, compromising its utility for district grid-interaction modeling and HVAC peak sizing.20 Integrating adversarial loss functions or physically constrained structural losses (e.g., Embodied Locomotion loss filters) preserves the high-frequency variance and stochastic diversity of predicted paths without sacrificing physical plausibility.59

### **Parameter Identifiability and Structural Unidentifiability**

Calibration of high-order multi-zone models often results in the issue of *parameter unidentifiability*.60 Due to the high dimensionality of supertall building models—which include hundreds of thermal zones, complex envelope properties, and highly uncertain occupant-driven schedules—multiple, distinct combinations of input parameters can yield identical output energy consumption curves.26 To diagnose and mitigate this issue, modelers utilize the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM).60  
The FIM represents the curvature of the negative log-likelihood function.60 The inverse of the FIM establishes the Cramér-Rao lower bound, indicating the minimum covariance matrix for any unbiased estimator of the parameters 60:  
![][image31]  
If the FIM is singular or has a very low determinant, it indicates that the parameters are structurally unidentifiable under the available metered data.60 Under these conditions, standard optimization algorithms will converge on physically unrealistic parameter values (e.g., pairing excessively high envelope infiltration rates with highly over-efficient mechanical systems to match a measured heating bill).60 Calculating the FIM using second-order differentiations allows modelers to isolate unidentifiable parameters with significantly fewer simulation runs compared to brute-force Monte Carlo or likelihood-ratio tests, indicating where supplementary sensor placement (e.g., localized sub-metering or CO2-based occupancy tracking) is required to constrain the inputs.26

## **Conclusions: A High-Fidelity Roadmap for Mixed-Use Supertall BPS**

To bridge the operational energy performance gap in vertically mixed-use supertall buildings, simulation practitioners and researchers must move beyond simplified, decoupled modeling assumptions. High-fidelity modeling requires an integrated framework that addresses the vertical microclimatic gradients, spatiotemporal occupancy transitions, core thermodynamics, and mathematical calibration constraints inherent to this typology.  
First, conventional ground-level weather files must be replaced with vertically resolved microclimatic boundary files that capture non-linear lapse rates and shear-induced wind pressures. Second, modelers must transition from static occupant schedules to shared-backbone Multi-Task Learning (MTL) architectures. This framework preserves spatiotemporal occupancy correlations across stacked functions while avoiding representation redundancy and occupant duplication.  
Third, vertical circulation shafts and mechanical service zones must be modeled as active thermodynamic elements. Co-simulation workflows linking EnergyPlus with CONTAM are essential to resolve stack-effect pressure dynamics and infiltration rates. Finally, calibration protocols must incorporate parameter identifiability checks using the Fisher Information Matrix. Enforcing these constraints prevents mathematical overfitting and ensures that energy conservation measures are simulated with physical validity, providing a reliable foundation for low-carbon design and grid-integrated operations in supertall developments.
